How I Did It: Space Defenders

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

1978, the year I opened, and Space Invaders was already the machine every kid in Portland wanted a turn on. I had a regular, a scrawny kid named Marcus who came in every day after school with exactly one quarter and somehow always beat his own score by ten points. There was a rival, a bigger kid, who'd lean on the cabinet and heckle him the whole time. Marcus never said a word back. Just kept shooting. One day the coin slot jammed on his last quarter and I fixed it for free and told him that one was on the house. He still beat his score.

What the remodel changed

The old version I built solo in '25 just moved everything the same amount every tick and called it a day — worked fine until somebody's laptop fan kicked on and the whole invasion sped up like they'd had too much coffee. This time the crew built it on "deltaTime," which just means the game asks the clock how much time actually went by and moves things by that much, so it plays the same speed everywhere. They also gave the invaders their real heartbeat back — that speeding-up thump as you thin out the ranks — using a little rising musical tone instead of one fixed beep, so the last invader standing sounds like it's panicking. And the shields chip apart properly now, a chunk at a time, not just a pixel here and there. Screen shakes when I get hit. That's the good stuff.

The spell that did it

Build Space Invaders against our shared GZ engine. Five rows of eleven invaders marching as one block, stepping down and reversing at the walls, speeding up as they thin out — classic heartbeat sound rising in pitch. One player bullet on screen at a time, no more. Four bunkers that erode in chunks from both sides, and the invaders should chew through them too as they march past. Random invaders drop bombs, a UFO crosses the top every so often for bonus points. Three lives, and make getting hit actually feel like something — shake the screen, blink me back in.

Under the hood

  • The whole invasion is one array of eleven-by-five invaders; every tick I check the leftmost and rightmost survivor against the walls before deciding whether to step sideways or drop down and reverse — same rule the original board used, near as I can tell.
  • March speed is computed fresh every tick from how many invaders are left alive, eased with a little curve so it's calm early and frantic at the end, and it slows back down a notch each time you clear a wave's worth and start the next, lower and meaner.
  • Bunkers are just a grid of tiny cells per shield. A hit erases a little blast radius of cells, not just one pixel, and I sweep the bullet's whole path each tick instead of just where it landed, so nothing skips through a thin sliver of shield by accident.
  • Only one column can ever fire down on you at a time from each row gap — I always pick the bottom-most survivor in a column to drop the bomb, which is the same trick that made the original feel fair even when it was trying to kill you.
